title: Holloman High Speed Test Track
description: There are very few missions requiring years of planning and preparation, only to be accomplished in less than six seconds. There are even fewer facilities where such a mission can take place.  The Holloman High-Speed Test Track, operated by the 846th Test Squadron, is one facility that enables test scientists and engineers to meet both of the above criteria. The test track is a 10-mile long, precision-aligned track that provides scientists and engineers a platform from which to conduct their various missions. Tests on the track provide valid data on problems which cannot be solved by other ground test means.
keywords: high speed, Holloman AFB, Test Track, Ejection seats, High Speed test track, new mexico

transcript.text: (engine roaring)
- We've reached velocities in excess
of 9,000 feet per second.
At this altitude, it's around mach 8.6.
The goal speed is posted all over our facility,
and that's mach 10.
(engine blasting)
(soft music)
So the Holloman High Speed Test Track
hearkens back to the 1950s.
- It's easy for me to look back
with a certain amount of nostalgia
and say ah, those were the good old days.
In a sense, they were, but look at the progress
that has been made since those so-called
good old days.
- If you look back in our history,
one of the hallmark figures
of the test track was Colonel Stapp.
So, he was secured in the sled
and was carried down the test track,
encountered water braking, which is a
common source to slow our sleds down,
and encountered in excess of 40 Gs in deceleration.
Missions changed over time, the track has changed
and it's grown from 3500 feet to 50,000 feet.
And now, of course, we're not strapping
live personnel to the track anymore.
We carry out egress missions,
but we use highly instrumented mannequins now
and all the data that can be collected on a mannequin,
you're just not gonna get with a human.
So, we collect the data.
We hand it off to human performance folks
who do the full-up evaluation.
- As we progress through generations
and different sizes of humans
to include now the female pilot force and smaller males,
we can test in these ejection seats,
reproduce those forces and ensure the safety
of the design down to the sizes
and up to the max size of current ejection seat occupants.
- Whenever there's a big change,
if you're adding weight to a helmet, for instance,
if you're changing your flight gear,
if you need to change a sequence,
or if you need to change components around the seat,
we need to check that out before
it's gonna be fielded out in fleet.
So, that's a large part of our job here
and drives our egress mission.
So, our impact to the Air Force
is directly supporting the war fighter.
And that is, what we're after
is to make sure if they have pull that handle
in the egress event
that, no kidding, they're gonna be as safe as possible.
That's what we're here to do
is to collect that data, verify that
everything has been accounted for
and that the seat is designed
in such a way to maximize survivability.
(soft music)
